primary_topics: Toast delivered at a tribute dinner for Secretary of Foreign Affairs Albert F. Del Rosario and Ambassador to Japan Manuel M. Lopez, May 3, 2011

The 'amortal' concept (coined by Time Magazine): today's 70-year-olds are the equivalent of yesteryears' 50-year-olds; life expectancy increases by two to five years per decade; happiness comes from adding life to years, not years to life; staying involved and chasing new aspirations

Manolo Lopez: CJP met him in early 2007 (two months after retiring as CJ) for lunch with Oscar M. Lopez and Eugenio Gabby L. Lopez III; offered independent directorship in First Philippine Holdings then Meralco (2008); his Japan earthquake-tsunami response as ambassador

Albert del Rosario: known CJP for three decades via monthly dinners with the late Doming Lim; Philippine Ambassador to the US (2001); resigned over the habeas corpus/emergency rule issue (2006); met again at PLDT, MPIC boardrooms; accepted Foreign Affairs post at CJP's urging
sub_topics: Why they accepted the call: 'they could not refuse the call of President Noynoy Aquino to help him win the war against corruption and poverty'; and 'they are merely changing tires prior to embarking on a new journey'

Amortal concept: 'a word coined by Time Magazine'; today's 70-year-olds are the equivalents of the yesteryears' 50-year-olds; 'the secret in adding life to our years is to stay involved, to continue to do what gives us fulfillment and pleasure, to construct a life full of attractions that we forget our calendar age and remember only to chase ever-new aspirations'

Manolo Lopez introduction: CJP first met him in early 2007 (two months after retiring); lunched with Don Oscar M. Lopez and Don Eugenio Gabby L. Lopez III; they invited CJP to be ID of First Philippine Holdings; in 2008, Manolo offered CJP another ID in Meralco (where Manolo was and still is chairman); 'privileged by birth, Manolo Lopez is a populist by choice'; 'highly principled but not haughty, self-propelled but not self-righteous, courageous but not pugnacious, prudent but not tentative, humble but not wimpy'

Manolo Lopez's Japan response: immediately upon arriving in Tokyo, 'seamlessly coped with the massive earthquake and tsunami that hit northern Japan'; 'personally supervised the relief and rehabilitation program for our overseas workers affected by this disaster'; 'journeyed to the disaster site personally with little regard for the possible effects of radiation on his own health'

Albert del Rosario introduction: known for three decades via monthly dinners with CJP and the late Doming Lim; 'we would then speak about the many challenges besetting the nation and our little dreams of contributing our bit'; Philippine Ambassador to the US (2001); 'his stint in the diplomatic corps came to an abrupt end in 2006 when he staunchly refused to support and, in fact, opposed the then administration's plan to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and to impose emergency rule'; went back to business; met CJP at PLDT, MPIC and other boardrooms; 'when President Aquino offered him to head the premier Cabinet post in the Foreign Service, I immediately urged him to accept'

Del Rosario's DFA first act: 'without much ado, he immediately flew to the Middle East several times to personally supervise the repatriation of our Overseas Filipino Workers who were trapped in the revolutions sweeping Egypt, Libya and other countries'; 'meet challenges head-on and hands-on and to take decisive, courageous and, yes, heroic actions to solve them, without TV cameras, press releases, fanfare and glitter'

stances.claim: The 'amortal' concept -- today's 70-year-olds are the equivalents of yesteryears' 50-year-olds, and life expectancy increases by 2-5 years per decade -- explains why both Manolo Lopez and Albert del Rosario left retirement to serve. 'Happiness lies not in merely adding more years to life, but, more important, in adding life to those years.' Service at 70+ is not sacrifice but fulfillment.
stances.rhetorical_move: amortal-as-vocation-framework: the Time Magazine concept as the philosophical justification for post-retirement public service
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing philosophical frame for the tribute

stances.claim: Albert del Rosario's 2006 resignation from the US ambassadorship -- 'when he staunchly refused to support and, in fact, opposed the then administration's plan to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and to impose emergency rule' -- is the defining evidence of his principled independence. CJP's endorsement of his DFA appointment is grounded in this specific act of courage.
stances.rhetorical_move: habeas-corpus-resignation-as-character-evidence: the 2006 resignation as the definitive proof of Del Rosario's integrity that justifies his appointment as Foreign Affairs Secretary
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's governing character assessment

notable_anecdotes: Manolo Lopez's Japan radiation courage: 'immediately and seamlessly coped with the massive earthquake and tsunami that hit northern Japan; personally supervised the relief and rehabilitation program for our overseas workers; journeyed to the disaster site personally with little regard for the possible effects of radiation on his own health.'

Albert del Rosario's 2006 stand: 'his stint in the diplomatic corps came to an abrupt end in 2006 when he staunchly refused to support and, in fact, opposed the then administration's plan to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and to impose emergency rule.' -- the most consequential personal sacrifice for principle cited in the corpus for a non-judicial figure.

The First Philippine Holdings ID origin story: 'I first met Manolo Lopez four years ago in early 2007, two months after I retired as Chief Justice of our country. Over lunch, he and the two other Lopez family patriarchs, Don Oscar M. Lopez and Don Eugenio Gabby L. Lopez III invited me to change tires and to begin a new journey as an independent director of First Philippine Holdings Corporation.' -- the precise first meeting that began CJP's corporate directorship career.

Monthly dinners with Doming Lim: CJP and Del Rosario 'used to dine monthly, along with a third friend Doming Lim who has now gone to the Great Beyond. We would then speak about the many challenges besetting the nation and our little dreams of contributing our bit to help solve them.' -- 30 years of shared civic dreaming.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 3, 2011 as a tribute toast for Secretary of Foreign Affairs Albert F. Del Rosario and Ambassador to Japan Manuel M. Lopez, this address by CJP opens with the philosophical frame: both men left retirement because 'they are merely changing tires prior to embarking on a new journey' -- justified by the 'amortal' concept (coined by Time Magazine) that today's 70-year-olds are the equivalents of yesteryears' 50-year-olds, life expectancy increases by 2-5 years per decade, and 'happiness lies not in merely adding more years to life, but, more important, in adding life to those years.' On Manolo Lopez: CJP first met him in early 2007 (two months after retiring as CJ) over lunch with Don Oscar M. Lopez and Don Eugenio Gabby L. Lopez III, who invited him to be an independent director of First Philippine Holdings; a year later (2008), Manolo offered him another ID in Meralco (where Manolo was and still is chairman). He describes Manolo as 'privileged by birth, a populist by choice... highly principled but not haughty, self-propelled but not self-righteous, courageous but not pugnacious, prudent but not tentative, humble but not wimpy'; his Japan earthquake-tsunami response saw him personally journeying to the disaster site 'with little regard for the possible effects of radiation on his own health.' On Albert del Rosario: known for three decades via monthly dinners with CJP and the late Doming Lim; served as Philippine Ambassador to the US (2001); resigned in 2006 'when he staunchly refused to support and, in fact, opposed the then administration's plan to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and to impose emergency rule'; met CJP at PLDT and MPIC boardrooms; 'when President Aquino offered him to head the premier Cabinet post in the Foreign Service, I immediately urged him to accept.' At DFA, he 'immediately flew to the Middle East several times to personally supervise the repatriation of our OFWs trapped in the revolutions sweeping Egypt, Libya and other countries... without TV cameras, press releases, fanfare and glitter.'
